chunks: Which motor temperatures matter. The question: Which temperatures do you want to/can you measure?
A motor has several different temperatures, and each one matters for a different reason. The copper winding matters most, because its insulation fails if it gets too hot.
In a permanent-magnet motor, the magnets matter too, because heat weakens them.
Bearings, brushes, the housing, and the drive's transistors (its electronic switches) each have their own limit. Some can be measured directly.
Others, such as a spinning rotor, must be estimated.
Think of a car. The engine coolant, the oil, the brakes, and the tires each have their own safe temperature, and each fails in its own way.
You read some from a gauge, but you can only guess the temperature of the tire's inner rubber.
A motor is the same: a set of parts, each with its own limit, and some parts you cannot reach with a sensor.
Heat sources feed a network of thermal resistances and capacitances. The winding is the hottest and fastest-changing node; the housing is the slowest and coolest.
Rotor heat leaves mainly through the air gap and shaft, which is why the rotor can run hotter than the stator in some designs, and why it is hard to measure.
Hot spot: the hottest point in the winding. It sets the insulation's life. Insulation class: a standard maximum winding temperature, such as class F at 155 degrees Celsius.
Remanence: the strength of a magnet's field. It falls as the magnet warms. Demagnetization: permanent loss of magnet strength from too much heat.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon inside a transistor. Thermal resistance: degrees of temperature rise per watt of heat flowing.
Neodymium (NdFeB) magnets lose about 0. 12% of their strength per degree.
Heat them by 100 degrees Celsius and the motor's torque per amp drops by 12%, so the motor needs about 13. 6% more current for the same torque.
Separately, a transistor carrying 20 amps through 8 milliohms dissipates 20 squared times 0. 008 equals 3. 2 watts.
With 30 degrees Celsius per watt of thermal resistance, its junction sits 96 degrees Celsius above the room, about 121 degrees Celsius in a 25 degrees Celsius room.
That is the whole idea: several limits, several sensors, plus some estimation.
"Several temperatures matter. The winding, average and hot spot, limits insulation life, so I embed a thermistor or use resistance.
The stator and housing lag but are easy to measure. For permanent-magnet motors the rotor magnets matter: NdFeB loses about 0.
1 percent flux per kelvin and can demagnetise, but you can't sense it directly, so I estimate it.
Bearings have a grease limit, brushes wear, and the MOSFET junction has to be computed from power and thermal resistance. Rotating parts need IR, telemetry or models."
